en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇapati. I study that speech of the All-pervasive Lord which is unutterable, yet replete with the repose of infinite powers contained within its beginning and end; it is the very heart of the Lord. (1)
He alone is the god Bhairava, and all the gods are composed of him;
she alone is that Bhairavī, and even existence and non-existence are composed of her.

That very Bhairava-knowledge, as well as that which consists of ignorance—even the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of which it consists—is indeed the established doctrine (siddhānta) of Bhairava. (3)
Wherein the six paths are unified, there is that state of Bhairavī;
at the limit of all tantras, she is the ineffable, supreme goal.
That state, in which will, knowledge, and action are submerged within the self that consists solely of consciousness and bliss,
is the heart of Bhairava, the God of gods, the ground of non-differentiation.
By virtue of his nature as consciousness, that Lord, the Sovereign, while reflecting upon himself,
attains the stages beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Bhūmi.
In that regard, within the Lord, who consists of both the signifier and the signified,
there exists a sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvatā*) corresponding to the sequential manifestation of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, occurring one by one in each of the two [aspects].
Sequence, which consists of space and time and has differentiation as its life-force, belongs to cognitions;
it is produced by the appearance of diverse forms due to the fragmentation of the cognizer.
In that regard, there are indeed two modes, distinguished by the pure and the impure self:
purity consists in the immersion of externalized objects into one's own "I-consciousness. (9)
Even for those submerged in impurity, there is no such rest for the heart;
even within this interval, there would be infinite states according to their relative degrees.
In the manifestation of these subjects according to what is appropriate or inappropriate for them, the commonality and the otherwise-being of the subject and the object are differentiated. // 11 //
That emission which has a clear manifestation free from conceptual construction is considered to be Śāmbhavī;
in the creation of oneself through non-duality, one's own self is made the instrument.

The power of consciousness, whose nature is action and knowledge, because it causes the threading together of distinctions, reaches the stage of *kalā* and *vidyā*, and thus undergoes the further emergence of differentiation. (13)
When the various modes of valid cognition consist of conceptualizations regarding an action,
that very [cognition] is an interrupted action whenever there is an exertion of knowledge.
When he has attained the state of being limited by the senses of action and intellect, he is then called a "bound soul" (paśu);
thus, through his own will, the Blessed Lord Bhairava is measured out [as such]. 15.
And that power, being of limited activity, follows him;
as his state of Śiva-hood—known as the attainment of the Vidyeśvaras—becomes contracted, he arrives at the status of a subject consisting of body, vital breath, intellect, and the void. (16)
Its uncommon creation consists of those various conceptual constructions;
it rests upon that [uncommon nature] for one who has been refined by the impressions arising from the Śiva-creation. (17)
This very cognizer, in this manner, remains undistracted within its own self— which is of the nature of non-conceptual consciousness— during the festival of perception.
My dear child, you yourself must perceive this: because the entire universe is known as non-dual consciousness, it is identical with that; anything else is trivial and unreal. (19)
What means could there be for this reality, since nothing other than it is possible?
This is a means that has no other means; they declare it to have itself as its own means.
Having withdrawn all thought from every quarter and cultivating the notion "I am," one attains non-conceptual self-awareness as a direct perception. // 21 //
Even when assuming these infinite forms, one should enter into that self-awareness which possesses a single characteristic and not conceptualize through conceptual constructions.
Having plunged into the Vyomeśvarī, which is one's own consciousness and a great lake filled by the flow of the four currents beginning with Khecarī, one should cause the dull-witted to feel ashamed.
Performing the fivefold acts in the sequence of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, suppression, and grace, one should have confidence that "I am Śiva."
Or else, by means of the sequence of emission, knowledge, discernment, and the flow of sound,
one who has integrated those [energies] within oneself through the mouth of the Guru shall become perfected.
Having conceptualized them, I, Bhairava, the soul of the universe, [perceive] those various manifestations of the universe as my very own,
just as the various forms of flames belong to fire and the various rays of light belong to the sun.

I alone possess the categories of the mother, consciousness, the means of knowledge, and the objects of knowledge; in the form of pure awakening and so forth, I am the fourteen [deities] beginning with Khecarī. // 27 //
Contemplating bondage and liberation through the modes of both difference and non-difference, one should, through the confidence that "I am Bhairava," attain supreme freedom of will. (28)

Since you, overflowing with sovereign power, impose upon yourself the internal and external activities without regard for temporal sequence and independent of any external cause, [you are truly the Lord]. (29)
The union is the emergence of rest within the self of the unsurpassed emission; it is the friction between Śiva and Śakti, and within that interval lie the other powers.

Bliss, will, and sovereignty are their unfolding; the deficiency of will and sovereignty, through the distinction between the unmanifest and the manifest, constitutes the manifestation of the object of knowledge for those two knowers. (31)
Through the two, bliss and the unsurpassed, there is then the state of union; as the vital breath of all that is to be felt, that body of Bhairava is complete. (32)
This radiance of the object of knowledge, situated as one within both Will and Sovereignty, attains the state of the five elements beginning with earth through its grossness. (33)

And through its subtlety, it then reaches the state of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with smell; and through contact with them as instruments, it attains the state of the ten sense organs (five each of cognition and action). 34.

Through the veiling of objectivity (vedyatā), in the process of manifesting subjectivity (vettṛtva), there arises the state of mind (manas) and the sense of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi); among these, when they are undivided, there is the state of primordial matter (pradhānatā) and the state of the person (puruṣatva), as well as contraction and expansion, all of which depend upon that [subjectivity]. (35)
They arose from the union of desire, which possesses a dual nature consisting of both [aspects],
due to the unfolding of the very essence of will, and otherwise, through its conjunction with the Absolute (Anuttara).

There are four powers residing within this person that support it from within; consisting of the nature of *māyā*, they bridge the void of consciousness and the realm of the insentient, like the triple-staffed pole of Triśaṅku.
From the threefold power of will (icchā-śakti), three other powers came into being;
then, through the expansion of that which is to be created, this emission (visarga) became exceedingly manifest.
Having created this through the mutual intermingling of its own powers, there may arise another state of agitation; however, this does not occur externally to emission (visarga).
All this, being existent, repeatedly comes to rest through the gateways of will and so forth within the unsurpassed Bhairava, and from that very state it is again emitted.
The supreme consciousness (*citi*) is the self-reflection upon its own nature, which contains within it infinite objects;
because it flows forth all at once, it is the mantra, speech, and pure agency. (41)

She herself draws forth Time—which flows in three ways, has three paths, and resides in three places—from within and then from without; thus, she is the venerable Parā, the Attractor of Time (Kālakarṣiṇī). 42.
The intermediate [speech] (parāparā), which perceives the differentiated internalized universal existence, is that very agency; it is Paśyantī when resting in the state of the Lord.
Madhyamā, which exists within the internal organ, is sequential and gross.
It is differentiated by conceptualization, distinct in its denotable objects, and divided by the fluctuations of the vital breath. // 44 //
Because one's own latent impressions remain as they were, even in the two preceding stages, there would be a limitation for the subject of Māyā; moreover, the transition to Paśyantī is gradual. (45)
Entering into those two stages in succession— the state of tranquility and the state free from conceptual construction— the fortunate one beholds with wonder the expansion of his own self-awareness.

Being of the nature of the activity of the vocal organs (*sthāna*), the articulatory efforts (*karaṇa*), and the impact (*āghāta*) [of the breath], she is *vaikharī*; these [other] modes of speech (*vṛtti*) of hers are within the range of hearing. (47)
Through these mutual transmissions of knowledge, there arises that worldly conventional practice, as well as the scriptural one, which is crowded with various limitations. (48)
Thus, even while he is awake, the goddesses headed by Māheśvarī— the presiding deities of these [five] groups— do not enjoy the one who knows this pervasion of speech.
One should practice non-grasping by means of the method, for the goal is the state of Bhairavī;
one should enter into that very self-consciousness which comprises all methods.
I take refuge in the unsurpassed splendor, the secret of mantras and mudrās, which is filled with infinite denotations and denotata contained within its beginning and end. (51)
Victorious are the ancient Gurus, whose hearts were inseparable from Śambhu,
and who attained the ultimate perfection of a samādhi from which there is no emergence.
Homage to Śiva.
This work, titled the *Paryantapañcāśikā*, is the completed composition of the venerable Abhinavaguptanātha.
